title: Chalmers University Demonstrates Hardware-Level Microwave Crosstalk Suppression via Parasitic Capacitance Engineering - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Chalmers University physicists show that microwave drive crosstalk in superconducting processors can be nulled by designing attofarad-scale parasitic capacitances so multiple drive paths destructively interfere, rather than by setting the coupler to Jeff = 0. On a two-transmon test chip the cross-Rabi minimum sat ~300 MHz from the Jeff = 0 point, and floating transmons proved far more fabrication-tolerant than grounded ones.

insights.claim: Chalmers researchers show that microwave drive crosstalk suppression in superconducting processors does not come from cancelling the effective exchange coupling (Jeff = 0) but from multi-path destructive interference among parasitic capacitive channels.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A standard superconducting chip-design heuristic is wrong, implying room for crosstalk gains via layout alone.
insights.locator: Physicists at Chalmers University of Technology

insights.claim: On a test chip with two fixed-frequency floating transmons (4.752 GHz and 4.658 GHz) and a flux-tunable coupler, the cross-Rabi crosstalk minimum occurred roughly 300 MHz away from the Jeff = 0 operating frequency of 3.665 GHz.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Empirical evidence that operating at Jeff = 0 leaves crosstalk performance on the table.
insights.quote: the cross-Rabi minimum occurred roughly 300 MHz away from the Jeff = 0 operating frequency (3.665 GHz)

insights.claim: Pulsing an XY drive line to control a target qubit induces spurious excitations and AC Stark phase shifts in neighboring 'victim' qubits, a key error source as superconducting processors scale.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Drive crosstalk is a scaling-limiting error that hardware vendors must solve to grow qubit counts.
insights.quote: pulsing an XY drive line to control a target qubit induces spurious excitations and AC Stark phase shifts in neighboring victim qubits

themes.theme: Parasitic capacitance as a design knob

insights.claim: Modeling the victim-qubit drive amplitude as a coherent sum of three channels (direct drive, stray drive-to-coupler capacitance of ~18-30 aF, and stray drive-to-victim capacitance of ~2-10 aF) lets designers size parasitics so the signals arrive with opposing phase and cancel completely.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Crosstalk can be engineered out at the layout stage rather than compensated with control electronics.

insights.claim: Engineering parasitic capacitances reduced unwanted victim-qubit state populations during single-qubit gates by orders of magnitude.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A potentially cheap, hardware-level route to higher single-qubit gate fidelity in dense chips.
insights.locator: Chalmers Two-Qubit Transmon Device & Crosstalk Model Parameters

themes.theme: Floating vs grounded transmons and ZZ alignment

insights.claim: Floating transmons have a pronounced practical advantage over grounded transmons for this technique: their crosstalk-null frequencies for opposing drive lines shift in the same direction as parasitics vary, giving lithographic leeway, whereas grounded designs need impractically tight fabrication margins.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Favors floating-transmon architectures for vendors pursuing passive crosstalk suppression.
insights.quote: The comparative analysis highlighted a pronounced practical advantage for floating transmons over grounded architectures.

insights.claim: Because tunable couplers have bias points where static ZZ interactions vanish, parasitic capacitances can be laid out so the classical microwave crosstalk null coincides with the quantum ZZ null at the same operating flux.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Simultaneously nulling classical and quantum crosstalk at one bias point simplifies calibration of larger processors.
